explain.say: Drop a tiny piece of lithium in water and it fizzes gently. Sodium whizzes about. Potassium bursts into a lilac flame! Why does each one get wilder? Look at the board, and you will see the reasons one by one.

explain.say: Five! Now look at this reason. The outer electron is far from the nucleus, and the inner shells get in the way. That is called shielding, like people standing between you and a magnet. So the pull gets weaker. Can you see why the electron might escape?

explain.say: Look at the graph. As you go down the group, reactivity climbs fast: lithium, sodium, potassium, then caesium. Each one loses its outer electron more easily, and losing it is how these metals react. Which one would you expect to be wildest?

The one at the bottom! Great work. Caesium explodes when it touches water, so these metals are kept under oil, away from air and water. Wow: you could cut them with a butter knife, and the fresh surface shines like silver, then dulls in seconds.

faq.q: Why does reactivity increase down group 1?
faq.a: Going down, atoms have more shells, so the single outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded. It is pulled less strongly and is lost more easily.
asks: Why is potassium more reactive than sodium?

faq.a: Shielding is when inner shells of electrons sit between the nucleus and the outer electrons, reducing the pull the outer electrons feel.

faq.q: What happens when sodium is put in water?
faq.a: Sodium floats, melts into a ball, fizzes and whizzes around, giving off hydrogen gas. The water left behind is alkaline, containing sodium hydroxide.

faq.q: Why are alkali metals stored in oil?
faq.a: They react quickly with oxygen and water vapour in the air. A layer of oil keeps air and water away.
asks: Why is sodium kept in oil?

faq.q: Why are they called alkali metals?
faq.a: When they react with water they make alkaline solutions, metal hydroxides like sodium hydroxide, plus hydrogen gas.
asks: What do group 1 metals make with water?

facts: Group 1 metals react with water to form a metal hydroxide and hydrogen, for example 2Na + 2H2O gives 2NaOH + H2.
Potassium burns with a lilac flame when it reacts with water.
